questions.prompt: Why does Pass the Hash work without the attacker ever knowing the user's actual password?
options: NTLM authentication proves knowledge of the password hash, not the cleartext password itself — possessing the hash is sufficient
Pass the Hash actually requires cracking the password first
It only works on accounts with no password set
Windows automatically resets passwords to a known default during the attack
questions.explanation: NTLM challenge-response authentication is built around proving knowledge of the hash, not the cleartext password — which is exactly what makes a stolen hash directly usable.

options: Using a hash so many times it becomes invalid
Using a captured NTLM hash to request a legitimate Kerberos ticket, then using Pass-the-Ticket with that ticket
A brute-force attack against NTLM hashes
Passing a hash between two different domains simultaneously
questions.explanation: Overpass-the-hash is the bridge technique: converting a stolen NTLM hash into a Kerberos ticket, then reusing that ticket via Pass-the-Ticket.

questions.prompt: Why do strong password complexity and rotation policies fail to prevent either Pass-the-Hash or Pass-the-Ticket?
options: These policies are actually effective against both techniques
Neither technique requires cracking or knowing the actual password at all — the hash or ticket is used directly
Both techniques only target accounts with weak passwords
Password policies only apply to local accounts, not domain accounts
questions.explanation: Both techniques reuse stolen authentication material directly — password strength is irrelevant since the password itself is never needed.

questions.prompt: What log correlation is described as the strongest signal for detecting either technique?
options: A single 4624 logon event alone, viewed in isolation
LSASS access immediately preceding an NTLM or Kerberos authentication event
Any successful logon during business hours
Password reset events occurring on a regular schedule
questions.explanation: LSASS access right before the authentication event is the strongest corroborating signal — it's how the hash or ticket was likely obtained in the first place.
